issues.legal_issue: The property-freedom guarantee does not apply where a tenant or licensee has been substantially deprived of the enjoyment of the property interest.
material_facts: The affected respondents occupied the requisitioned premises as tenants or a licensee.
Requisition removed the right to occupy and the rights to transfer, assign, let, or sublet, leaving only the residual title to the leasehold interest.
issues.conclusion: Article 19(1)(f) did not apply to the respondents because the requisition substantially deprived them of the rights normally associated with their interests in the premises.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 19(1)(f) and 31 address different fields and do not overlap. Article 19(1)(f), read with clause (5), presupposes property over which the relevant rights can be exercised; when substantial deprivation removes the normal attributes of enjoyment and leaves only a husk of title, Article 31 governs. The Court relied on A. K. Gopalan v. State of Madras, The State of West Bengal v. Subodh Gopal Bose, and Dwarkadas Shrinivas of Bombay v. The Sholapur Spinning and Weaving Co. Ltd.

predicates.challenge_to_property_requisition: A claimant challenges a government order requisitioning property.
predicates.claimant_holds_a_tenancy_or_license_inte: The claimant occupies or holds an interest in the property as a tenant or licensee.
predicates.normal_property_enjoyment_rights_are_sub: The measure removes the ordinary rights of enjoyment associated with the claimant’s interest, leaving only a residual or nominal interest.

issues.definition: When a requisition challenge concerns a tenant or licensee whose ordinary property enjoyment rights have been substantially removed, the property-freedom guarantee does not apply.

issues.legal_issue: A requisition law is not invalid merely because it does not state the precise purpose for which each property may be taken, where its scheme indicates a state or public purpose and it provides compensation.
material_facts: The principal requisition law predated the Constitution, while its duration and relevant provisions were extended or amended after the Constitution came into force.
The law provided for compensation and its amended provisions authorized requisition for a state or other public purpose.
The law did not specify the precise purpose for each requisition.
issues.conclusion: The Act was not invalid for failing to state the precise purpose for which property was being taken.
issues.legal_principle: For Article 31(2), the statute need not expressly state the precise purpose of taking property if its overall tenor and intendment show that the taking is for state purposes or for the public benefit. The Court relied on The State of Bihar v. Maharajadhiraja Sir Kameshwar Singh of Darbhanga.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_requisition_: A person challenges the validity of a law authorizing government requisition of property.
predicates.law_provides_compensation: The law provides compensation for property requisitioned under it.
predicates.statutory_scheme_indicates_state_or_publ: The law’s overall text and scheme indicate that requisition is for state purposes or public benefit.

issues.definition: A challenged requisition law that provides compensation and indicates a state or public purpose is not invalid merely because it omits the precise purpose of an individual taking.

issues.legal_issue: Omitting the public purpose from a requisition order does not invalidate the order when the purpose is established by other evidence.
material_facts: The initial orders requisitioned premises without stating the purpose.
Later orders and affidavits on behalf of the government stated that the premises were requisitioned to house people without accommodation.
Evidence described an acute housing shortage and the public problems associated with homelessness.
issues.conclusion: The omission of the purpose from the initial orders was not fatal because the public purpose was established through other evidence.
issues.legal_principle: A requisition order need not itself state the purpose if the facts establishing that purpose are shown to the court in another way. The Court applied the underlying principle of Biswabhusan Naik v. The State of Orissa.

predicates.challenge_to_requisition_order: A person challenges a government order requisitioning property.
predicates.order_omits_its_purpose: The requisition order does not state the purpose for which the property is taken.
predicates.public_purpose_established_by_other_evid: Evidence outside the order establishes that the requisition serves a public purpose.

issues.definition: If a challenged requisition order omits its purpose but other evidence establishes that purpose as public, the omission does not invalidate the order.

issues.legal_issue: Requisitioning vacant premises to house genuinely homeless people serves a public purpose, and government may reasonably select beneficiaries under a general allocation policy.
material_facts: The government requisitioned premises amid an acute housing shortage, in part associated with an influx of refugees.
The government had used first informants to identify suppressed vacancies and allotted some such premises to informants who genuinely needed accommodation.
The allocation policy was intended both to house homeless people and to encourage disclosure of vacancies; no fraud, invidious discrimination, nepotism, bribery, or corruption was alleged.
The shortage required selection among many homeless applicants, and the government considered practical and public-policy factors in choosing an allocation scheme.
issues.conclusion: Housing a person without accommodation was a public purpose, and the challenged requisition and allotment orders were not ultra vires on the ground that the beneficiary was a first informant or that another allocation method might have been preferable.
issues.legal_principle: A public purpose is fulfilled when requisitioned accommodation is allotted to a person who is in fact homeless. Government has wide discretion to implement the statutory policy and may choose among reasonable allocation schemes; courts do not substitute a different scheme merely because it may seem preferable. A particular allotment may be challenged on grounds such as fraud, invidious discrimination, nepotism, bribery, or corruption.

rule.if: challenge_to_requisition_or_allotment and accommodation_allocated_to_a_genuinely_homeless_person and allocation_uses_informant_status and selection_follows_a_reasonable_general_policy and no_improper_selection_is_shown

predicates.challenge_to_requisition_or_allotment: A person challenges a government requisition or the allocation of requisitioned accommodation.
predicates.accommodation_allocated_to_a_genuinely_h: The recipient of the accommodation in fact has no housing accommodation.
predicates.allocation_uses_informant_status: The allocation scheme considers whether a person identified a previously undisclosed vacancy.
predicates.selection_follows_a_reasonable_general_p: The government selects recipients on broad principles and through a reasonable policy suited to the circumstances.
predicates.no_improper_selection_is_shown: The challenger does not establish fraud, invidious discrimination, nepotism, bribery, corruption, or comparable improper selection.

issues.definition: A challenged requisition and allocation serve a public purpose when accommodation goes to a genuinely homeless person under a reasonable general policy, including one that considers informant status, and no improper selection is shown.

issues.legal_issue: A person challenging an apparently authorized requisition order bears the burden of proving its illegality, particularly when the disputed facts are especially within that person’s knowledge.
material_facts: The challengers alleged that the premises did not meet the statutory description of premises that could be requisitioned because they had not been let or intended to be let.
The government’s order appeared on its face to be within its statutory authority and to comply with the statute.
Whether the premises had been let or were intended to be let was a matter on which the challengers had special means of knowledge.
The government declined to lead evidence on that issue, and the High Court placed the burden on the government.
issues.conclusion: The High Court placed the burden of proof wrongly; it was for the challengers to show that the apparently valid order was illegal.
issues.legal_principle: A party who alleges that a government order is illegal must establish that illegality when the order is facially authorized and prima facie compliant with the statute. This is particularly so where the disputed matter is within that party’s special means of knowledge.

predicates.challenge_to_government_requisition_orde: A person challenges a government order requisitioning property.
predicates.order_appears_authorized_and_compliant: The order appears on its face to fall within government authority and to comply with the governing requirements.
predicates.challenger_has_special_knowledge_of_disp: The facts disputed as a basis for alleging illegality are especially within the challenger’s knowledge.

issues.definition: When an apparently authorized and compliant requisition order is challenged over facts especially known to the challenger, the challenger bears the burden of proving illegality.
